html:
The Scythians and Saka were Iranian-speaking mounted nomads who ruled the Eurasian steppe from the Black Sea to the Altai mountains from about the 9th to the 3rd century BCE. Greeks called the western groups Scythians; Persians and Indians called the eastern ones Saka. They were never one state but a cultural zone with many rulers.

They were among the first peoples to fight mainly as mounted archers. In the 8th century BCE they pushed the Cimmerians off the Pontic steppe, and in the 7th century they raided deep into West Asia, until the Medes drove them back.

Neighbours wrote about them often:

  • Herodotus described their customs and the failed campaign of Darius the Great against them around 513 BCE.
  • The Achaemenid Empire listed several Saka peoples among its subjects and soldiers.
  • Greek cities on the Black Sea traded grain and gold with them.

Their tombs are famous for gold work in an animal style, like the Golden Man of Issyk in Kazakhstan, and for frozen burials in the Altai with tattooed bodies, felt and horses.

In the west, the Sarmatians overcame the Scythians in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. In the east, Saka groups moved south into Bactria and India, where they ruled as the Indo-Scythians before the Kushans rose.
